Author: @CoffeeTech101
Content:
I was a nvidia fan for a long time.... up until 5 days ago when my nephew bought a 5060 and asked me to install it in his B450 motherboard with a ryzen 5 in it.   Now call me crazy but usually a card upgrade is pretty straight forward,  uninstall previous drivers, turn off system, pull out old card, put in new card, turn on system, install drivers, and go back to gaming.    Yea,  that didn't happen with the 5060. Installed card,  installed drivers, windows 10 crashes,  restart sends into black loop of hell.   Go into safe mode, uninstall drivers, system functions like normal.  Rinse and repeat.   Look online and alot of other people having similar problems with not only the 5060, but ALL the 5000 series and certain motherboard chipsets.    

5 hours later after a bios update, windows updates, trying things like switching pcie to gen 3 from gen 4, trying different drivers and a few other recommendations...... still doesn't work.   

Took it back, got a 9060 xt 16gb, plugged it in, installed adrenaline drivers, off to the races.   

I don't know what the hell nvidia is thinking but if they continue on this path they're going to lose customers.   

Normal people aren't going to troubleshoot for 4 hours trying to figure out why their system went crazy, they just want something that works and something as minimalistic as a video card upgrade shouldn't cause that kind of grief for people.

Author: @RFC3514
Content:
I'm pretty sure "no compromise" in that paragraph is about the 16 GB model (i.e., you get more VRAM if you play games that need it while getting the same GPU). The 8 GB model is the one with a "compromise" (i.e., meant only for 1080p "e-sports" - read Counter-strike), in exchange for a lower price. AMD probably makes about the same on both models, assuming the GPU itself is exactly the same; the price difference will be up to the card manufacturers, how much the VRAM costs, and how much they save in manufacturing.

I think you're so used to Nvidia completely controlling its AIBs that you assume AMD can do the same. They can't; they represent less than 20% of the discrete GPU market. Prices and models are going to be determined (or at least heavily influenced) by the card manufacturers.

Author: @devilmikey00
Content:
The thing I hate most about this "8GB is enough for 1080p" is that it's a bunk argument to begin with. It assumes that resolution is the end all be all of keeping within a VRAM buffer. 1080p in 2025 is not the same as 1080p in 2016 when the 1060 came out. Many many options are just as or more demanding on VRAM in modern games as resolution. If a game is running at the same settings and you only change the resolution to 1440p or 4k the difference isn't going to be 8gb, it's going to be 2-4gb. Which is why 12gb runs 1080p games flawlessly regardless of settings while 8gb requires multiple compromises. 

This is also going to get worse because, as we've seen in the last 8 months or so, more and more games are coming out without the option to fully disable RT effects. RT gobbles up VRAM far worse than resolution does. This is only going to get more and more common with each release as devs streamline their workload to stop supplying two bespoke lighting solutions for every title. I mean RT's been around for 6 years, the transition has to happen at some point. Whether hardware is ready or not doesn't mean squat to publishers because they really don't care if a game runs well or not. Turn on DLSS or FSR if you want 30 fps is all they'll say.  

Also, the focus on "esports titles" is also BS. A toaster can run those in excess of 100 FPS at 1080p. You don't need a new card for that. Literally any video card made since 2019 can blast through Esports games. It's a nonsense talking point. Hell, if you buy a now nearly 10 year old 1080ti you'd tear through every single esports title and you'd get 11gb of ram to boot. The Esports gamer doesn't need to upgrade unless they are running something incredibly low end. What would these 8gb cards even be an upgrade from? They run about just as well as 3060ti from 4 years ago and that had a 12gb model. They'd be better off buying one of those used. Or you know, consoles and phones also have most esports titles and run them just fine because, again, a toaster can run them.

So, this entire conversation comes immediately from a place of dishonesty and hyper focuses on something that's not as relevant as they'd like you to think (resolution) or are already completely irrelevant (esports discussion) and will become more and more irrelevant going forward. I hate all of it, the whole conversation is crap and everyone just goes along with the faulty framing AMD/Nvidia is pushing for justifying 8gb in 2025.

Author: @FrancisFjordCupola
Content:
I think tech review sites are really just a bit stupid and click-baity. With VRAM capacity it's all good until you run out of VRAM. So the real question is: when and where does that happen? Then from that, it is a question of whether or not it's acceptable. If you're mainly looking for a new GPU to play out the whole Steam backlog, 8GB is plenty enough. If the main example is 4K ray-tracing on Cyberpunk... going from 15.4 fps to around 8 fps... I'd want neither. But I'm also wary of the settings used. I run a simple 6600 and with that and a bit of tuning it can do 1080p with medium RT at 60 fps. And it looks and feels good. Testing should be done at realistic settings.

I do think people should future-proof themselves with 16Gb cards if they can. Consoles have that amount of memory, so one can expect a tendency to use that amount of RAM. But it is entirely overblown. Generally speaking, the 16Gb versions provide more bang for the buck.
